details: is a privately held company founded in 1999 by Raymond C. Kurzweil, an author, inventor, and futurist. He's perhaps best known for creating an optical character recognition system that – in conjunction with a flatbed scanner and text-to-speech synthesizer – reads text aloud to the sight-impaired. FatKat is an acronym derived from "financial accelerating transactions from Kurzweil Adaptive Technologies". The aforesaid company is one of a total of nine Kurzweil companies. The purpose of FatKat as listed with the Massachusetts Secretary of the Commonwealth Corporations Division is "investment software". Kurzweil, who specializes in artificial intelligence coupled with pattern recognition, has created software that uses quantitative methods to pick stocks for investment purposes. Although selecting stocks based on software-generated recommendations is not new, FatKat's approach was unique at the time because of its "nonlinear decision making processes more akin to how a brain operates". The software can evolve by creating different rules, letting them compete, and using (or combining) the best outcomes. explainer.lead: FatKat is investment software created by FatKat, Inc., a privately held company founded in 1999 by Raymond C. Kurzweil. It uses quantitative methods and evolving decision rules to select stocks, with an approach described at the time as nonlinear and more akin to how a brain operates.

tiers.eli5: Imagine several helpers trying different recipes for choosing stocks. FatKat lets their ideas compete, keeps or mixes the ideas with the best results, and can keep changing its rules. The goal is to improve software-generated investment recommendations rather than follow one fixed recipe.
tiers.practitioner: FatKat applies quantitative stock-selection methods through candidate rules that compete, with the best outcomes used or combined. Its notable design idea is adaptive, nonlinear decision-making rather than a fixed recommendation rule. Its brain-like description should not be treated as a specification of a neural architecture or a guarantee of investment results.
tiers.paperLevel: FatKat is a quantitative stock-selection system whose decision rules can evolve: generate candidate rules, evaluate them through competition, then use or combine the best outcomes. Its originating company, FatKat, Inc., was founded by Raymond C. Kurzweil in 1999. The phrase 'nonlinear decision making processes more akin to how a brain operates' characterizes the approach without specifying a formal mathematical model.

explainer.example: Imagine three candidate rules produce different sets of stock picks. If two produce the best outcomes in the competition, FatKat can use or combine those outcomes, then base later recommendations on the improved decision process.

usedIn.detail: Applies quantitative methods and evolving decision rules to investment decisions.

explainer.intuition: Instead of relying on one permanent stock-picking rule, FatKat treats rules as candidates that can compete and change. Useful outcomes survive or are combined, allowing the software's decision process to evolve.
howItWorks: Apply quantitative methods to the stock-selection problem.
Let the candidate rules compete by their outcomes.
Use or combine the best outcomes.
explainer.whyItMatters: FatKat shows how pattern-recognition and adaptive-rule ideas can be applied to financial decision-making. Its rule competition offers an alternative to keeping one fixed quantitative stock-picking procedure.
misconceptions: FatKat is not Kurzweil's reading system for sight-impaired users; that earlier system combines optical character recognition, a flatbed scanner, and text-to-speech synthesis.
Its brain-like description does not establish that it is a literal simulation of a brain.
